title: Kisa Gotami's child
hookLine: a young mother carries her dead son from house to house, asking for medicine

lines: WHEN A LOSS CAN'T BE ACCEPTED YET.
A MOTHER, GOING DOOR TO DOOR.
cards: This story is sad, and it's told gently. Grief can have a stretch where the loss can't be accepted yet. The phone number stays saved.
A place gets set at the table out of habit. Surely, the mind says, something can still be done. A young woman named Kisa Gotami stands in a city street, a small boy on her hip.
He's her only child. He's just learned to walk. And he has died.
She won't put him down. She goes from door to door, asking everyone she meets for medicine.

teach.b: Her story is told in the commentaries, the explanations written down alongside the old texts, and her own poems survive among the verses of the elder nuns. Her name is part of the story.
Kisa means thin: she was Gotami, and people called her the thin one. Born into a poor family, she married into a wealthy house, and the story says her husband's family looked down on her.
Then she had a son, and everything changed. She was honored now. She belonged.
The child was her place in the world as much as her joy. And then he died, very young. So she lifts him onto her hip and walks.
Can you give me medicine for my son? People stare. Some laugh at her.
Who has ever heard of medicine for the dead? She keeps walking. She carries him everywhere.

The story doesn't call her foolish, and it doesn't rush her. It lets her be refused, house after house, because this is what grief does: the mind can't take in the loss all at once, so it goes looking for a way around it.

Finally someone sees her differently. A wise man, the story says, understands that she's out of her mind with grief, and doesn't mock her. I don't have medicine, he tells her, but I know someone who might.

So she carries her son to where the Buddha is teaching, stands at the edge of the crowd, and asks him: do you know a medicine for my child? i'll stop there for today, with her question. Tomorrow, his answer.

how: Buddhist teachers retell Kisa Gotami's story at funerals and in times of grief, and her own verses are preserved in the Therigatha, the poems of the elder nuns.

o: a queen who gave the first monastery its land
a goddess of the harvest in village shrines
a young mother whose name meant the thin one

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.

s: Kisa Gotami's story is told in the commentaries
the fuller story is in the commentaries; her own verses are in the Therigatha.
the story calls her foolish for asking
it lets her walk and be refused, because that's what grief does.
the wise man mocked her like the others
he saw her grief and sent her to the Buddha.

games.q: a young mother stops you in the street, holding her dead child, asking for medicine. what do you do?
o: laugh. there's no medicine for the dead.
tell her gently where she might find help.
games.why: many turned away or laughed. one wise man saw her grief and sent her to the Buddha. tomorrow, what he says.

practice: Think of someone you know who is grieving, recently or long ago; maybe it's you. You don't have to fix anything or find the right words: just picture sitting beside them, the way a friend sits at a hospital bed.
Let your breath be slow and steady, as if you were breathing for both of you, and stay.

wordCard.voice: Kisa Gotami. The thin Gotami, a young mother carrying her dead son from door to door, asking for medicine.

orig.note: Pali: thin, lean. Kisa Gotami: the thin Gotami.

carryVoice: Your line: she carried him everywhere. The story simply lets her walk. Seventy-four days in.
